newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Prosperous HK set for emotional return to China.
newsitem.headline: Prosperous HK set for emotional return to China.

text.p: Communist China will receive intact one of the most powerful financial centres in the world this week when Britain surrenders Hong Kong -- its last major colonial outpost.
For a week Britain has succumbed to nostalgia, with a string of "End of Empire" celebrations to bring down the curtain on more than 150 years of rule on the south China coast.
Home to 6.4 million people, Hong Kong was seized by Britain in 1841 as a safe-haven for opium traders and became a financial powerhouse in the 1970s and 1980s.

During the past week kilted bagpipers have played "Amazing Grace", military bands have belted out "Land of Hope and Glory", and Prince Charles has taken up residence in Hong Kong harbour on the royal yacht Britannia.
For the departing colonial rulers the moment is packed with emotion. Chris Patten, the 28th and last British governor, had to wipe a tear from his eye during one reception.

The ceremonies reach their finale at midnight (1600 GMT) on Monday when Prince Charles yields the fiercely capitalist and wealthy colony to China's President Jiang Zemin in Britain's most significant colonial surrender since India in 1947.
The moment is charged with emotion for China and Chinese residents of Hong Kong as well.

"As a Chinese I am proud to see the closing of the colonial era, which began with pain and ends with pomp and pageantry," said lawmaker David Chu at the final session of the colonial assembly on Saturday.
Dazzling rival fireworks displays will light up Hong Kong, one to say farewell and the other to celebrate reunification on Monday, and 4,000 guests will join the gala handover ceremonies.
China's celebrations will just be starting and will go on for 24 hours while Prince Charles, along with Patten, sail off aboard the Britannia and leave Hong Kong in Chinese hands.
For Beijing that moment erases 156 years of national shame and reintegrates into the mainland a financial centre which is expected to vigorously promote China's economic development.
Hong Kong industrialists have already moved aggressively into southern China for their manufacturing needs, setting up operations which employ an estimated five million Chinese.

Since 1979 when China's late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping opened up the country of 1.2 billion people and its economy to the world, foreign investment has soared to nearly $100 billion. Two out of every three dollars has come through Hong Kong.
Diplomats and bankers have said the reintegration of Hong Kong into China will speed regional economic development, and accelerate the infrastructure projects which go with it.

Despite concerns among many over China's decision to curb democratic reforms introduced in the twilight of British rule, the Hong Kong business community is riding a wave of optimism and sees the transfer bringing even greater wealth.
The Hang Seng share index soared in the run-up to the June 30 handover and finished on Friday at an all-time closing high of 15,196.79 points.

Land and rent prices, already astronomical, have risen even further as Chinese rule approaches and there has been no sign of panic flights of capital or people which have occurred at times in the past.
Diplomats and bankers have said that the only cloud on Hong Kong's horizon is the shadow cast by Beijing over the territory and how heavy a hand it will try to play in internal affairs.
Under a 1984 Sino-British deal, Hong Kong will be a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China and its internal affairs should be left largely alone for the next 50 years.

But China sent jitters through Hong Kong by making clear the territory will be under its sovereignty and announcing plans to send in 4,000 People's Liberation Army (PLA) troops, with armoured cars and helicopters, shortly after the handover.

"China's decision ... on this point (troop deployment) is an assertion that behind Hong Kong's autonomy there will always be the very heavy hand of Chinese control," Rory Mungoven, from the Amnesty International human rights group, said.

China has the right under the 1984 treaty to deploy as many troops as it likes for national defence but human rights groups reacted angrily to the 21 armoured cars crossing the border six hours after the handover.

The quick deployment has prompted memories of the PLA's role in crushing a student uprising in Beijing 1989 with a heavy loss of life. That, in turn, triggered a flight of people and capital from Hong Kong.
Attention has been focused on Tung Chee-hwa, the shipping magnate who was picked by Beijing to be the new chief executive in Hong Kong, replacing Patten.
Tung has curbed some political reforms, limiting protests and stopping foreign financial support for Hong Kong's political parties.
He has said that while criticising local issues was okay, championing causes which anger Beijing, such as independence for Taiwan or Tibet, would not be tolerated.
